source_text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with FCC structures have excellent properties, such as mechanical and irradiated properties at room temperature [,, ] What is more, porous high-entropy alloys are acted as efficient electrocatalysts that has a potential application [,, ]. While, strength drops obviously in FCC HEAs at high temperature (>800 °C). To explore HEAs with stable properties at high temperature, many researchers have focused on refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that are composed mainly by refractory alloys. Xiong et al. explore the response of WTaTi, WTaCrV, and WTaCrVTi under He implantation and compare the results with pure W, which proposes higher irradiation resistance in RHEAs than in W. Radiation-induced amorphization of RHEA is reported and the finding challenges the current understanding of phase stability of RHEAs upon irradiation. In Li's research, self-healing behavior are observed in TiTaNbZr films that was revealed on account of the enhanced diffusion and redistribution of atoms, which could also lead to a decrease of irradiation defects. What is more, functional W composites are successfully justified as potential applications in radiation shielding field [,,,, ].

NbZrTi-based HREAs are widely well studied [,,,, ], for example, Pu et al. reveal that irradiation-enhanced surface blisters in TaTiNbZr RHEA were strongly dependent on He plasma energy. In Chang’ results, the swelling and hardening effects in HfNbTaTiZr RHEA were significantly suppressed compared to those of conventional nuclear materials. According to the structural stability under high temperature irradiation, significant irradiation-enhanced precipitation with Hf and Zr enrichment is observed in HfNbZrTi RHEA.

To improve stability at high temperature, Senkov et al. successfully prepared equal atomic ratio NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with single-phase BCC structure in 2010. These RHEAs possess excellent mechanical properties at high temperature (1600 °C). In addition, Ren et al. assumed high irradiation-resistance in NbMoTaW RHEA by first - principle calculations. However, the ductility of NbMoTaW RHEA at room temperature is pretty bad, which is similar to tungsten alloys and molybdenum alloys. Lots of researches have shown that the addition of rhenium (Re) can effectively reduce the ductile-brittle transition temperature of W and Mo, and improve the room temperature strength, elongation and irradiated properties, which is also called as “rhenium effect”.

The “rhenium effect” methods have been successfully applied to NbMoTaW RHEAs. For example, Zhang et al. justified that ductility at room temperature increases from 2.6 % in NbMoTaW to 7.0 % in NbMoTaWRe0.5. Zhang et al. verified the addition of Re did not affect the single-phase BCC structure in multi-elements RHEAs. In addition, the addition of Re is also beneficial to irradiation-resistance in Mo alloys and W alloys, which may make NbMoTaW RHEA excellent mechanical and irradiation properties.

queries.broad: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.
queries.problem_constrained: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its high irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Earlier rhenium-based work increased NbMoTaW room-temperature elongation from 2.6% to 7.0% without changing its single-phase BCC structure, while irradiation benefits were reported for tungsten and molybdenum alloys rather than demonstrated for NbMoTaW. Other refractory high-entropy alloys have shown higher resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation, but also irradiation-induced amorphization, energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation, indicating unresolved stability risks. Given the need to retain BCC structural stability and high-temperature performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

leaks.why: It directly identifies rhenium as the relevant intervention class, strongly pointing to Re addition to NbMoTaW.
